entries.clue: Jumpy character from Disney (New York) about to pull film on Hendrix? (6,7)

indicatorNotes.on: Read across the grid, what is written on something has been come to after it, so the pieces stacked on Hendrix follow him rather than lead.

blocks.note: the guitarist's first name
ny = New York
c = circa, the Latin for about
to rick a muscle is to pull or wrench it
E.T., the Spielberg picture

annotation.surface: Disney's New York office is on the point of dropping a documentary about Hendrix.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Film' sounds like part of the Disney story and is the Spielberg title instead. 'About' is the Latin circa, one letter, and 'pull' is the wrench you give a muscle.
annotation.definitionFit: Jiminy Cricket is Pinocchio's top-hatted conscience in the Disney film, and the cricket half of him is an insect built for jumping.

entries.clue: Large bowl and jug once repaired using mucilage first of all (5)

indicatorNotes.first of all: First of all means before anything else, so only the letter each word opens with is wanted.

blocks.note: the opening letter of each of the five words, taken in the order they are written

annotation.surface: A jug mended long ago with plant glue.
annotation.walkthrough: Mucilage is the sticky gum plants exude, used as glue. 'Repaired' sits exactly where an anagram indicator would sit and is only fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: A jorum is a large drinking bowl, and by extension the quantity of punch it holds.

entries.clue: Old rocker's rival holding drill for bike (5)

indicatorNotes.holding: To hold something is to have it inside your grip, so the letters named next sit within the ones before them.

blocks.note: in 1960s Britain the Mods and the Rockers were rival youth tribes who brawled at seaside resorts
pe = physical exercise, the school lesson once called drill

annotation.surface: An ageing rocker's old enemy clutching a power tool.
annotation.walkthrough: The Mods rode scooters and the Rockers rode motorbikes, so the rivalry in the surface is quietly about machines. 'Drill' is the gym lesson, not the thing in the toolbox.
annotation.definitionFit: A moped is a small motorised two-wheeler with pedals, and 'bike' is what anybody riding one would call it.

entries.clue: Set-up that's not working on Souness? Yes, it seems, periodically (9)

indicatorNotes.periodically: Something done periodically happens at regular intervals, which here means taking letters at a fixed step instead of all of them.

blocks.note: every second letter of the run, starting from the second

annotation.surface: Someone agreeing that whatever was tried on Souness has failed.
annotation.walkthrough: Graeme Souness is the Scottish footballer turned manager and television pundit, here only for his letters. The count runs straight through the punctuation, which is what makes the step hard to hold.
annotation.definitionFit: A non-system is an arrangement that is no arrangement at all, which is what a set-up that does not work amounts to.

entries.clue: Soup, something to eat with wine coming up (7)

indicatorNotes.coming up: In a down entry a piece coming up is read from the bottom towards the top, so its letters arrive in the opposite order.

blocks.note: chow is slang for food, as in chow time
the wine is red, set climbing

annotation.surface: Soup, and a snack to go with the wine being fetched up from the cellar.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Coming up' does the cellar's work in the surface and a turnaround's in the wordplay. Only three letters of the answer are actually reversed, which is why the front half reads so innocently.
annotation.definitionFit: Chowder is a thick soup of fish or clams with potato and milk, so 'soup' names the kind of thing it is.

entries.clue: Elected Conservative is capping yellow tooth (7)

indicatorNotes.capping: A cap goes on the top, and in a down entry whatever caps something is written above it.

blocks.note: a candidate who wins is in
c = Conservative, the party label on a ballot paper
the word taken exactly as it stands
or is the heraldic name for gold or yellow

annotation.surface: A newly elected Tory having a yellowing tooth capped.
annotation.walkthrough: Or is heraldry's gold, and the heraldic colours are worth learning as a set alongside argent, sable and gules. 'Capping' is the dentist's word in the surface and a placement instruction underneath.
annotation.definitionFit: The incisors are the flat cutting teeth at the front of the mouth, so 'tooth' names one of them plainly.

entries.clue: Dutch boat's paperwork officer grabs (4)

indicatorNotes.grabs: To grab something is to close your hand round it and keep it there, so the words named are holding the letters wanted inside them.

blocks.note: four consecutive letters straddling the join between the two words

annotation.surface: An officer seizing a Dutch vessel's documents.
annotation.walkthrough: A koff is a broad, flat-bottomed Dutch coaster, so the boat in the surface and the boat in the answer are the same sort of thing. Watch where 'paperwork' ends.
annotation.definitionFit: A koff is a two-masted Dutch coasting vessel, beamy and flat-bottomed — a boat, and a specifically Dutch one.

entries.clue: Fancy solitude, beginning to yawn as if boring (9)

indicatorNotes.Fancy: To fancy something up is to dress it differently, and letters dressed differently come out in an order they were not given in.
indicatorNotes.beginning to: What a word is only beginning to do it has barely started, so nothing but its opening letter counts.

blocks.note: eight letters of fodder
the first letter of the word, taken because the clue asks only for its start

annotation.surface: Imagining time alone, and starting to yawn at the thought of it.
annotation.walkthrough: The yawn is the joke: the clue makes you drowsy while telling you the answer means drowsy-making. 'Fancy' is an anagram indicator far more often than it is a verb meaning want.
annotation.definitionFit: Tediously is the adverb for doing a thing in a way that bores people, which is what 'as if boring' describes.

entries.clue: Flat racing here, short guy and small horse failing to finish (5)

indicatorNotes.short: A word given short is cut off before it ends, giving up its final letter.
indicatorNotes.failing to finish: A runner failing to finish never reaches the end, and neither does the word — its last letter is left off.

blocks.note: to guy somebody is to rib them, and that three-letter verb is docked
a small horse is a pony, one letter short of home

annotation.surface: A short man and a small horse that pulled up before the line.
annotation.walkthrough: Ripon is a North Yorkshire racecourse given over to flat racing, and 'here' is the setter pointing at a place rather than naming it. 'Guy' looks like a bloke and is the verb meaning to tease.
annotation.definitionFit: Ripon's course runs flat racing and nothing else, so 'here' defines the town by what happens at it.

entries.clue: Imagined monster lurking inside covered entrance (3)

indicatorNotes.lurking inside: Something lurking inside stays in the middle and out of view, so the letters at each end of the word are not part of what is wanted.

blocks.note: a covered entrance is a porch, and only what sits between its two ends survives

annotation.surface: A creature out of somebody's imagination skulking in a doorway.
annotation.walkthrough: The hiding place is not in the clue's own letters: you have to turn 'covered entrance' into a single word first, and only then look inside it.
annotation.definitionFit: Orcs are the goblin-like foot soldiers of Tolkien and the fantasy writing after him, monsters that exist only in fiction.

entries.clue: Loudly unwrapped cheap sweet (5)

indicatorNotes.unwrapped: Unwrapping takes off whatever is round the outside, so the word loses the letter at each end.

blocks.note: f = forte, a score's direction to play loud
cheap is budget, stripped of the letter at each end

annotation.surface: A cheap sweet being noisily unwrapped.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Loudly' is the musician's f, not a signal that something is to be heard — the pull towards a sound clue is the whole trap. Cheap has to become budget before anything can come off it.
annotation.definitionFit: Fudge is the soft sweet boiled from sugar, butter and milk, so 'sweet' names the kind of thing it is.

entries.clue: Earl left church recess with special passes (7)

blocks.note: e = earl in the peerage
l = left
the apse is the rounded recess at a church's east end
s = special

annotation.surface: An earl walking out of a church alcove carrying something out of the ordinary.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Left' looks like the verb driving the sentence and is a single letter. An apse is standard crossword furniture, and so is the peer supplying an E.
annotation.definitionFit: Time elapses means time passes, and both verbs carry the same third-person s.

entries.clue: Obscure 1970s glam rock band with Wizzard and Roxy, both at the end (5)

indicatorNotes.both at the end: 'Both' points back at the two names just given, and 'at the end' takes nothing but what each of them finishes with.

blocks.note: Mud were a British glam band of the mid seventies, remembered for Tiger Feet
the closing letter of each name, in the order given

annotation.surface: Naming a half-forgotten glam band alongside Wizzard and Roxy Music.
annotation.walkthrough: Wizzard and Roxy Music were the famous glam acts of exactly those years, so the third band is hidden inside its own company. 'Obscure' reads as how well known the band is and means unclear.
annotation.definitionFit: Muddy water is water you cannot see through, and 'obscure' carries that sense of unclear rather than of little known.

entries.clue: Unhappy about hotel's Scotch (4)

indicatorNotes.about: Turning about faces the other way, so the letters just named are read back from their far end.

blocks.note: unhappy is sad, turned about
h = hotel in the radio alphabet

annotation.surface: Somebody grumbling about the whisky a hotel serves.
annotation.walkthrough: The capital S sells the whisky and hides a verb: to scotch a plan is to kill it off. Hotel is H because the radio alphabet gives setters a letter for every word in it.
annotation.definitionFit: To scotch a rumour is to put an end to it, and to dash somebody's hopes is the same destroying act.

entries.clue: Batty individual in sitcom that's British and not American (4)

annotation.definition: Batty individual in sitcom that's British

blocks.note: nor is the single word that says and not
a = American

annotation.surface: A dotty character in a comedy series made in Britain rather than the States.
annotation.walkthrough: Nora Batty, played by Kathy Staff, was the wrinkled-stockinged terror of Last of the Summer Wine, the BBC's long-running comedy about three old men loose in the Yorkshire hills. Batty is her surname.
annotation.definitionFit: Nora is the forename of Nora Batty, and the sitcom she stands in is as British as they come.

entries.clue: Ref nuts to wave card? (7)

indicatorNotes.to wave: To wave a thing is to shake it to and fro, and letters shaken to and fro do not land in the order they started in.

blocks.note: seven letters of fodder

annotation.surface: A furious referee brandishing a card at somebody.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Card' is the referee's yellow one in the surface and the old compliment in the answer — calling somebody a real card. 'Nuts' looks exactly like the anagram indicator and is fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: A card, in the old idiom 'he's a real card', is an amusing joker, which is precisely what a funster is.

entries.clue: Mad and brilliant (7)

blocks.note: read as furious rather than insane — a temper gone up to full heat
read as blazing bright rather than clever — the light a fire gives off, not the wit

annotation.surface: A back-handed verdict on somebody both unhinged and gifted.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves come from the same fire, one from its heat and one from its light, which is why the clue can get away with three words. In Britain the word also does duty as a mild swear — a flaming nuisance.
annotation.definitionFit: Flaming means raging, as a temper does, and it also means blazing or gaudily bright, which is the brilliance of a burning thing.

entries.clue: Sustenance provided by fresh trout in inn, tail removed (9)

indicatorNotes.fresh: A fresh arrangement is a different one, so the letters are laid out again rather than kept as given.
indicatorNotes.tail removed: The tail is the end, and removing it drops the final letter off the run just named.

blocks.note: the three words run together give ten letters, and the last of the ten goes

annotation.surface: A fresh trout served at an inn with its tail cut off.
annotation.walkthrough: The trim is the cook's job in the surface and the letter count's job underneath — leave it in and there is one letter too many. 'In' is fodder, not an instruction to insert anything.
annotation.definitionFit: Nutrition is the nourishment a body draws from what it eats, which is what 'sustenance' names.

entries.clue: Changes player on pitch to face Sweden (7)

blocks.note: re = on the subject of, as at the head of a memo
to pitch a ball is to cast it
s = Sweden, the country's international vehicle plate

annotation.surface: A squad member out on the field preparing to play Sweden.
annotation.walkthrough: Every word of the football is busy elsewhere: 'on' is the memo's re, 'pitch' is the verb meaning throw, and Sweden is one letter off the back of a car.
annotation.definitionFit: To recast is to put a different actor into a part, so a director who recasts is changing a player in the cast.

entries.clue: One shooting curvaceous feature on a model perhaps (6,3)

annotation.definition: One shooting curvaceous feature on a model perhaps

blocks.note: the surface offers a photographer at work; the setter means the winged archer of myth, and it is the weapon being named rather than the archer himself

blocks.clueFragment: curvaceous feature on a model perhaps
blocks.note: anatomy borrows that same name for the double curve of the upper lip, the feature a glamour model is admired for

annotation.surface: A photographer capturing a model's curves.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition given twice, once out of mythology and once out of the beauty column. 'Perhaps' is there because a model is only one example of somebody with such a lip.
annotation.definitionFit: A cupid's bow is the weapon the love-god shoots arrows from, and in anatomy the double curve of an upper lip named for that shape.

entries.clue: Have a go at tango, mostly unoccupied (7)

indicatorNotes.mostly: Mostly is not wholly, so the word hands over all of itself but the last letter.

blocks.note: the word stands as its own two letters
t = tango in the radio alphabet
unoccupied is empty, cut short

annotation.surface: Trying out the tango in a room with hardly anybody in it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'At' looks as though it belongs to the definition — have a go at something — and supplies the first two letters instead. A dance named in a clue is nearly always the radio alphabet's T.
annotation.definitionFit: To have a go is to attempt something; the two verb phrases swap straight over in casual English.

entries.clue: Large wave ruined suit upset man's wearing (7)

indicatorNotes.ruined: Something ruined has lost its shape, so its letters will not stay in the order they were handed over in.
indicatorNotes.upset: In a down entry upset means tipped over, so those letters are read from the bottom up.
indicatorNotes.wearing: You wear a garment by being inside it, so the man goes within the other letters rather than beside them.

blocks.note: the four letters of the garment, ruined into a new order and left open in the middle
the wearer, tipped upside down

annotation.surface: A big wave has wrecked the suit an unhappy man had on.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface makes the wave the vandal and the answer is the wave, so the definition is standing inside its own story. 'Upset' means overturned here, not annoyed.
annotation.definitionFit: A tsunami is the huge sea wave thrown up by an earthquake or a landslip, so 'large wave' names it by size.

entries.clue: Dad possibly sent back lots of fruit? (7)

indicatorNotes.sent back: Something sent back returns the way it came, and across the grid that means reading its letters right to left.

blocks.note: papa is dad
say means possibly, as in 'say, on Tuesday', and it is turned round

annotation.surface: A father who may have returned a large quantity of fruit.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' looks like the setter hedging and is a word in its own right: say, meaning for instance. The question mark covers a plural defined as a quantity.
annotation.definitionFit: Papayas are the orange-fleshed tropical fruit, and the plural answers the clue's 'lots of'.

entries.clue: Academic researcher's job, as before, essentially sucks (7)

indicatorNotes.essentially: The essence of a word is its very middle, so nothing but the central letter is taken.

blocks.note: a post is a job
do is ditto, written down a list to mean the same as before
the middle letter of the five

annotation.surface: Complaining that a research job is as dismal now as it ever was.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Do' for ditto is old ledger shorthand, a column of entries reading do., do., do. 'Sucks' is modern slang in the surface and nothing but a five-letter word underneath.
annotation.definitionFit: A postdoc holds a postdoctoral research position — an academic researcher past the PhD and short of a permanent job.

entries.clue: Flag Iraqis ignoring a question (4)

indicatorNotes.ignoring: To ignore something is to leave it out, so the letters named after it never get written down.

blocks.note: the nationals, with two of their six letters struck out
the letter A itself, and it goes
q = question, as in Q and A, and that goes too

annotation.surface: Singling out the Iraqis who are refusing to answer.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flag' is the plant and not the banner: the wild yellow iris that grows in wet ground has been called a flag for centuries. Q for question comes from Q and A.
annotation.definitionFit: The waterside iris is commonly called a flag, a name much older than the crossword and still used by gardeners.

entries.clue: Copper, extremely suspicious and stubborn sort (4)

indicatorNotes.extremely: The extremes of a word are its two ends, so its first and last letters are the pair being asked for.

blocks.note: cu is copper's symbol in the periodic table
the letter at each end of the word

annotation.surface: A policeman, deeply wary, and an obstinate character.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Copper' is the metal and not the policeman the surface is selling you; the periodic table hands setters Cu, Fe, Sn and Pb over and over. 'Extremely' never means very in a cryptic.
annotation.definitionFit: A cuss is a fellow or a creature, usually an awkward one — the sense in 'a stubborn old cuss'.

entries.clue: Given drugs, idiot sped regularly by day (5)

indicatorNotes.regularly: Letters taken regularly are taken at an even step through the words rather than all of them.

blocks.note: every second letter across the pair of words, starting with the second
d = day

annotation.surface: A fool on drugs who kept driving too fast in daylight.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Regularly' reads as how often he sped and is the instruction to skip letters. The definition is the opening phrase, which looks like a description of the idiot rather than the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: To be dosed is to have been given a dose of medicine or drugs, the past participle matching the clue's 'given'.

entries.clue: Make fun of our company overturning honey (5)

indicatorNotes.overturning: What is overturned ends up the other way up, so everything assembled before it is read back.

blocks.note: to rag somebody is to make fun of them, as in a students' rag week
the company we make between us

annotation.surface: Mocking our firm for knocking the honey over.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Honey' and the answer are both what you call somebody you are fond of, which is how the definition sits so quietly at the end. 'Our company' is simply us.
annotation.definitionFit: Sugar and honey are both endearments, so calling somebody sugar is calling them honey.

entries.clue: Condemns Wall's on the radio (5)

indicatorNotes.on the radio: On the radio you are heard and not seen, so what matters is the sound of the word and not the way it is written.

blocks.note: a wall thrown across a river is a dam, so the possessive in the clue belongs to a dam, and that sound has a second spelling with a silent letter in it

annotation.surface: A broadcaster laying into the ice cream firm.
annotation.walkthrough: Wall's is the British ice cream and sausage brand, which is what the capital letter is selling you. The apostrophe is not decoration — it stays in the spoken version, and only the spelling changes.
annotation.definitionFit: To damn something is to condemn it outright, the verb a critic reaches for when damning a play.

entries.clue: Withdrawing part of uptight aesthete in Bottom (4)

indicatorNotes.Withdrawing: To withdraw is to draw back the way you came, so the letters found are read in the reverse direction.
indicatorNotes.part of: Only a portion of the words that follow is wanted, and it is a run taken straight out of them.

blocks.note: four letters run straight across the join between the two words, and are then turned round

annotation.surface: A tense aesthete drawing back inside Bottom.
annotation.walkthrough: The italics push Shakespeare's weaver at you and the definition wanted is the everyday bottom, the part of you that meets a chair. Nothing in the clue is an anagram, though 'uptight' is doing its best to look like one.
annotation.definitionFit: A chair's seat is what your bottom rests on, and 'seat' is itself the polite word for the bottom.

entries.clue: Lead in Evita backing stagehand's complaint (5)

indicatorNotes.Lead in: The lead is whatever comes first, so only the letter the name opens with is taken.
indicatorNotes.backing: To back something is to stand behind it, so that letter is written after the word it is supporting.

blocks.note: a grip is the stagehand who shifts scenery and rigs the camera
the first letter of the title, which is all the clue asks for

annotation.surface: The star of Evita standing behind a grumbling stagehand.
annotation.walkthrough: The italics mark Evita as the musical, whose title is wanted for one letter only. 'Lead' reads as the leading role and means the leading letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A gripe is a grumble or grievance, the noun you get from griping about something.

entries.clue: Help professional to cover piano (3)

indicatorNotes.to cover: To cover a thing is to put it out of sight, so the letter named next is hidden away rather than written down — a loose use, since covering more often means wrapping round.

blocks.note: a professional army is a paid one and professional work is paid work, and that four-letter word goes one letter lighter
p = piano, the score's direction to play soft, and that is the letter put out of sight

annotation.surface: Lending a professional a hand to get the cover onto a piano.
annotation.walkthrough: Piano is the musical p for soft, the quiet twin of the f that opens 10 across. Getting from 'professional' to paid is the step the surface works hardest to hide.
annotation.definitionFit: To aid somebody is to help them, and the noun aid is help as well, so the swap works either way round.

entries.clue: Expression of surprise and cheers heard when introducing Seal (2,3)

indicatorNotes.heard: A word heard rather than read gives up only its sound, which may well be written another way entirely.
indicatorNotes.introducing: To introduce somebody is to bring them on first, so the piece named goes in front of the other.

blocks.note: in Britain cheers does duty as a casual goodbye, and that farewell said aloud can be written two letters shorter
to gum an envelope down is to seal it

annotation.surface: A gasp and a round of cheering as the singer Seal is brought on.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer is a northern English exclamation, a minced oath politely standing in for something stronger. The capital on Seal is the singer, and the verb underneath is what you do to an envelope.
annotation.definitionFit: By gum! is what a Yorkshireman says on being astonished, a softened substitute for swearing by God.

entries.clue: Get to the point: new town's crime down after outlaw finally leaves (3,5,5)

indicatorNotes.new: A new arrangement is a different one, so the letters are set down in an order they were not given in.
indicatorNotes.finally: Finally points at the end of the word, so its closing letter is all that is meant.
indicatorNotes.leaves: What leaves is no longer there, so that letter is not among the ones you write down.

blocks.note: the three words run together, with the W of the last of them struck out
its closing letter is the one that goes

annotation.surface: A new town reporting its crime figures falling once the last outlaw moved away.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Down' is part of the fodder rather than a direction, which is the hardest thing to see in a thirteen-letter shuffle. 'Outlaw finally' names a letter, not a person walking out.
annotation.definitionFit: To not mince words is to say the thing plainly with nothing softened, which is exactly what getting to the point means.
